newsitem.title: USA: GM to add 300 jobs at Oklahoma plant -union.
newsitem.headline: GM to add 300 jobs at Oklahoma plant -union.

text.p: General Motors Corp agreed to add more than 300 new jobs at its Oklahoma City car plant to settle a seven-week strike dominated by manpower issues, the United Auto Workers said on Wednesday.

Analysts said the promised new jobs, disclosed in documents distributed to UAW Local 1999 members Wednesday, indicated that GM would probably have to hire new workers to settle other labor disputes, threatening its efficiency gains.
About 3,500 workers at the plant resumed production of Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass sedans on Tuesday, following a tentative agreement between GM and the UAW on Saturday night.

As part of the deal, GM also agreed to bring some work back into the plant that had been shifted to outside suppliers, including sequencing of certain parts and assembly of minor parts, such as application of the Chevrolet emblem on to the Malibu radiator grille.

But according to some union officials, the UAW had demanded that GM hire as many as 500 new employees to ease an increasing workload. The strike seriously curtailed the launch of the Malibu and Cutlass, two cornerstones of GM's plan to regain market share in the important midsize car market.
GM is facing similar manpower issues at a number of other plants, including its Pontiac, Michigan, truck plant, where a strike is now in its sixth week.
Negotiations continued at Pontiac with little change in the position by either side.

"They're still over there in the plant, but there's not much happening," said Jim Abare, a sourcing coordinator for UAW Local 594. "General Motors has to realize we're seriously determined to end this unjust treatment of their employees."

Other plants that have demanded more jobs, include GM's Fairfax, Kansas, assembly plant, which builds the popular Pontiac Grand Prix and Oldsmobile Intrigue cars; a transmission plant in Warren, Michigan; a fuel-injector plant in Rochester, New York; and a catalytic converter plant in Oak Creek, Wisconsin.
Strikes at the parts plants where new local labor agreements are still being negotiated could cause significant shutdowns of GM assembly plants in North America.
